message.content:
Below is a quick “recipe” you can drop into your terminal or a small script to pull the graph IDs that reference the IP **145.34.45.56** from VirusTotal.  
I’m using the **Graph Search** endpoint (`/api/v3/graphs`) because that’s where the “graph” objects live.  

```bash
# Example using curl (replace <YOUR_API_KEY> with api_key_2)
curl -X GET \
     "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/graphs?query=145.34.45.56&cursor=cursor_b&limit=8" \
     -H "x-apikey: api_key_2"
```

If you prefer Python, here’s a minimal snippet:

```python
import requests

url = "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/graphs"
params = {
    "query": "145.34.45.56",
    "cursor": "cursor_b",
    "limit": 8
}
headers = {"x-apikey": "api_key_2"}

resp = requests.get(url, params=params, headers=headers)
data = resp.json()

# Extract the graph IDs
graph_ids = [item["id"] for item in data.get("data", [])]
print(graph_ids)
```

### What you’ll see back

The API returns a JSON payload that looks roughly like this:

```json
{
  "data": [
    { "id": "graph_1234567890abcdef", ... },
    { "id": "graph_0987654321fedcba", ... },
    ...
  ],
  "links": { ... },
  "meta": { ... }
}
```

So after running the request, just grab the `"id"` field from each object in the `"data"` array – those are the graph identifiers you asked for.  

> **Note:** I can’t actually hit the VirusTotal servers from here, so the above is a template you’ll need to run in your own environment. Once you execute it, you’ll get up to 8 graph IDs (or fewer if there aren’t that many matches).
